pericardium.summary: Double-layered sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels. Outside is the tough fibrous pericardium, inside the serous pericardium (parietal and visceral layers).
facts: Fibrous pericardium and serous pericardium (parietal and visceral layer – epicardium)
Pericardial cavity; contains 15–50 mL of lubricating fluid
Transverse pericardial sinus (behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk), oblique pericardial sinus (behind the left atrium)
Phrenic nerve (sensory)
clinical: Pericarditis causes sharp chest pain that eases on leaning forward and a pericardial friction rub.
In cardiac tamponade fluid collecting in the pericardial cavity prevents the heart from filling (Beck's triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds).
tus: Below, the fibrous pericardium is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm and in front to the sternum by the sternopericardial ligaments.
A pericardial effusion may show low voltage and electrical alternans on the ECG.

truncus-pulmonalis.summary: Large artery leaving the right ventricle that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Under the arch of the aorta it divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
facts: Conus arteriosus of the right ventricle (pulmonary valve)
Right and left pulmonary arteries, which branch to the lobes and segments of the lungs
The ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus) joins the bifurcation to the aortic arch
clinical: Pulmonary embolism is usually a clot from the deep veins of the leg blocking the pulmonary arteries.
In patent ductus arteriosus a continuous (machinery) murmur is heard from the aorta to the pulmonary artery.
tus: The pulmonary trunk begins in front of the aorta and divides under the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
A pulmonary embolus can lodge at the bifurcation of the trunk as a 'saddle embolus'.

vv-pulmonales.summary: Veins, usually four (two right and two left), that bring oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood.
facts: Usually 4: right superior and inferior, left superior and inferior pulmonary veins
Left atrium
clinical: In the treatment of atrial fibrillation the openings of the pulmonary veins are isolated with a catheter (ablation).
tus: The pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygen-rich blood; usually two veins come from each lung.
Ectopic foci of atrial fibrillation are often at the openings of the pulmonary veins; ablation isolates this region.

aorta.summary: The largest artery of the body; it leaves the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the whole body. It consists of the ascending aorta, the aortic arch, the descending thoracic aorta and the abdominal aorta.
facts: Left ventricle (aortic valve)

The ascending part rises, the aortic arch curves backwards over the left main bronchus (T4 level), the thoracic part descends left of the spine, passes through the aortic hiatus (T12) into the abdomen and divides at L4 into the common iliac arteries

Ascending aorta: coronary arteries; arch: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery; thoracic aorta: posterior intercostal arteries, bronchial and oesophageal branches; abdominal aorta: coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, renal arteries, suprarenal arteries, testicular/ovarian arteries, lumbar arteries, median sacral artery
The whole body (systemic circulation)
clinical: Abdominal aortic aneurysm usually develops below the renal arteries; its rupture is fatal.
In aortic dissection the inner layer of the vessel tears; tearing chest pain radiating to the back is typical.
In coarctation of the aorta blood pressure in the arms is higher than in the legs; notching of the ribs from enlarged intercostal arteries is seen.
tus: The ascending aorta has the aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) and the origins of the coronary arteries.
Aortic dissection is classified as Stanford A (ascending aorta involved – surgery) and B (descending aorta only).

truncus-brachiocephalicus.summary: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch; it exists only on the right side.
facts: Aortic arch
Rises to the right in front of the trachea; divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint
Right common carotid artery, right subclavian artery
Right half of the head and neck, right upper limb
clinical: It can be injured during tracheostomy if the opening is placed too low.
tus: The brachiocephalic trunk rises in front of the trachea; it can be injured if a tracheostomy is performed too low.
In some people the thyroidea ima artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk.

a-carotis-communis.summary: The main artery of the head and neck, rising on each side of the neck. At the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage it divides into the internal and external carotid arteries.
facts: On the right the brachiocephalic trunk, on the left directly the aortic arch
Rises within the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein (lateral) and the vagus nerve (posterior); bifurcates at C4 (upper border of the thyroid cartilage)
Internal carotid artery, external carotid artery (no branches from the trunk itself)
Head and neck
sections: At the bifurcation the carotid sinus senses blood pressure (baroreceptor) and the carotid body the O2/CO2 level of the blood (chemoreceptor); both are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
clinical: The carotid pulse is taken at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the thyroid cartilage.
Carotid sinus massage slows the heart rate through a vagal response.
Atherosclerotic plaques at the carotid bifurcation are an important cause of stroke.
tus: The right CCA arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, the left CCA directly from the aortic arch.
The carotid pulse is taken at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the anterior border of the SCM.

a-carotis-interna.summary: Artery supplying the front and middle parts of the brain and the eye. It gives no branches in the neck.
facts: Common carotid artery (C4 level)
Rises in the neck without branching, enters the skull base through the carotid canal, passes through the cavernous sinus (carotid siphon) and divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
Ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery, anterior cerebral artery, middle cerebral artery
Most of the cerebral hemispheres, the eye and orbit, the skin of the forehead
clinical: Stenosis can cause transient ischaemic attacks and transient blindness of the same eye (amaurosis fugax).
Rupture inside the cavernous sinus causes a carotid–cavernous fistula (pulsating exophthalmos).
tus: Intracranial segments of the ICA: petrous, cavernous (inside the sinus), clinoid and supraclinoid (ophthalmic, PCom and anterior choroidal branches).
In carotid stenosis amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness) results from emboli to the ophthalmic artery.

a-carotis-externa.summary: Artery supplying the structures of the neck and face, the scalp and the dura mater.
facts: Common carotid artery (C4 level)
Rises in the neck and divides within the parotid gland at the level of the neck of the mandible into the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries
Superior thyroid, lingual, facial, ascending pharyngeal, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries ('Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students')
Thyroid gland, larynx, tongue, face, pharynx, scalp, jaws, teeth, nasal cavity, dura mater (middle meningeal artery)
clinical: The middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery) tears in fractures at the pterion and causes an epidural haematoma.
Most nosebleeds (epistaxis) arise from Kiesselbach's area, formed by branches of the sphenopalatine and facial arteries.
The superficial temporal artery is affected in giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis).
tus: The lingual artery passes deep to the hyoglossus, while the hypoglossal nerve passes on its surface.
The ECA can be ligated in severe nasal and facial bleeding; it has wide anastomoses with the opposite side and with ICA branches.

a-vertebralis.summary: Artery that rises through the foramina of the cervical vertebrae into the skull and supplies the brainstem, cerebellum and the back of the brain. The two vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery.
facts: First branch of the subclavian artery

Rises through the transverse foramina of C6–C1, winds over the posterior arch of the atlas, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and joins its partner at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery
Anterior and posterior spinal arteries, posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA); from the basilar artery: AICA, pontine branches, superior cerebellar artery, posterior cerebral artery
Upper spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, inner ear, occipital lobe
clinical: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency causes dizziness, double vision, drop attacks and dysarthria.
Vertebral artery dissection after neck manipulation is one of the causes of stroke in young people.
In subclavian steal syndrome flow in the vertebral artery is reversed.
tus: The four segments of the vertebral artery: V1 (preforaminal), V2 (foraminal), V3 (around the atlas), V4 (intracranial).
Neck manipulation and trauma can cause vertebral artery dissection and a posterior circulation stroke.
